codes.sample: None. This is an editorial overview of a theme issue that summarises other articles. It has no participants or data of its own.
codes.instruments: None
codes.possible_duplicate: None. Two articles in the theme issue cover misophonia: Mednicoff et al. [19] (an online study of misophonic adults, likely a selected sample) and Berger et al. [20] (a theoretical paper). They may need to be screened separately.
codes.note: An editorial introduction to the Phil Trans R Soc B theme issue 'Sensing and feeling'. Misophonia is described only in narrative summaries of other papers ('Misophonia is characterised by strong negative emotional reactions to certain sounds'). There are no prevalence data or counts.

codes.sample: No participant sample. This is a narrative review of the neuroanatomy and pharmacology of the sympathetic pathways that control the pupil, drawing on animal and human studies.
codes.instruments: None. The paper reports no misophonia measure; its methods are pupillometry and pharmacological studies cited from the literature.
codes.note: The full text was retrieved. The paper covers light-inhibited and light-stimulated sympathetic pupil pathways (the locus coeruleus and dorsal raphe nucleus), not misophonia. It is also a review with no primary data, so E4_design would apply as well. The only mention of sound is the acoustic startle reflex in fear conditioning.

codes.sample: Retrospective cohort of 72 inpatients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (16 men, 56 women) treated at the National Hospital of the Ministry of Health of the Kyrgyz Republic, 2021–2024.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The study used medical record review and EDSS. Misophonia is not measured.
codes.note: This study looks at sex differences in multiple sclerosis (MS) and does not assess misophonia. The only mention of misophonia is in reference 6 (Kenar SG et al., 'The effect of misophonia on the severity of depression and anxiety in multiple sclerosis', Turk J Neurol 2022;28:24-30). That cited study recruited an MS sample and may be eligible, so it is worth checking for the review.

codes.sample: International identification survey (n=312 respondents) and interim prioritisation survey (n=327), plus a UK workshop (n=21). Respondents were people with hyperacusis, parents/carers, family, and educational and healthcare professionals.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The surveys asked open-ended questions about research uncertainties in hyperacusis and then asked people to vote on their top questions (JLA priority-setting).
codes.note: This is a James Lind Alliance priority-setting partnership on hyperacusis research. Misophonia comes up only to tell it apart from hyperacusis, and misophonia uncertainties were excluded as out of scope ("uncertainties about misophonia or recruitment alone"). Misophonia was not assessed and there are no misophonia counts. The consensus design could also justify E4_design.

codes.sample: One patient: a 72-year-old woman seen at the European Hospital Tinnitus Center for severe hyperacusis, photophobia and skin hypersensitivity.
codes.instruments: No misophonia-specific instrument. The clinicians concluded "hyperacusis and misophonia (Jastreboff category 4)". Other measures: Khalfa hyperacusis questionnaire, ULL, audiometry, PSQI, SCL-90-R, EPQ, BDI and STAI.
codes.note: This is a single-patient case report. Misophonia comes up only as a clinical conclusion ("Our conclusion was that the patient suffered from hyperacusis and misophonia (Jastreboff category 4)"). The report gives no prevalence data and no sample denominator.

codes.sample: None. This is a historical column about Paul E. Meehl, clinical versus statistical prediction, and predictive modelling. It has no participants.
codes.instruments: None. It does not mention misophonia.
codes.note: This is a historical and theoretical column in Harvard Review of Psychiatry (2023). It is unrelated to misophonia or sound sensitivity and reports no empirical data. If the topic did not rule it out, E4_design (theoretical paper or commentary) would also apply. The full text was available.

codes.sample: UK Biobank GWAS of de novo tinnitus (19,907 severe tinnitus cases, 114,930 controls), compared with cancer survivor cohorts (Platinum Study, CCSS-Rad-study).
codes.instruments: Self-report tinnitus item (UK Biobank); SCIN tinnitus item; physician-diagnosed tinnitus self-report. No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This is a genetic association study of tinnitus. The text never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or sound intolerance.

codes.sample: None. This is a scoping review of 55 otolaryngology studies that used IRT or Rasch analysis. It has no primary participant sample.
codes.instruments: None administered. Table 1 lists an included study (Vitoratou et al. 2021, n = 613, UK) that used 'Individual misophonia auditory triggers'.
codes.possible_duplicate: Cites Vitoratou et al. 2021 (2PL IRT, n = 613) on individual misophonic triggers. That primary study should be checked on its own if it is not already in the screening set.
codes.note: This is a scoping review of IRT methods in otolaryngology, so it reports no primary misophonia prevalence data. Misophonia comes up only in Table 1: 'To examine individual misophonic triggers ... Individual misophonia auditory triggers' (Vitoratou et al. 2021, n = 613).

codes.sample: 65 children aged 6-14 yr (24 with DCD, 41 TD); final analysed sample 15 DCD and 31 TD; recruited via university advertisements, social media and clinicians (Melbourne, Australia).
codes.instruments: BOT-2 SF, DCD-Q, ADHD-RS, hand rotation task (motor imagery), T1-weighted MRI. No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: The study is about motor imagery and gray matter volume in children with developmental coordination disorder. The full text never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or sound tolerance.

codes.sample: 60 children aged 4–12 with normal hearing (Italy): 30 with DSM-5 ADHD combined presentation and 30 healthy controls matched for age and sex.
codes.instruments: Hyperacusis parent questionnaire (PQ) and children's interview (CI), adapted from Coelho et al. (2007) and translated into Italian. Neither is specific to misophonia: the items cover sensitivity to everyday or loud sounds, and the CI asks about 20 sounds that contain no mouth or nose trigger sounds.
codes.note: Only hyperacusis was measured (PQ >8 plus CI positive with 5 or more annoying sounds; 11/30 ADHD, 4/30 controls). Misophonia comes up only in the limitations section: "the study design does not allow differentiation between hyperacusis, misophonia and phonophobia". No misophonia-specific case definition.

codes.sample: None. This is a consensus-based clinical practice guideline for tinnitus (TINNET COST Action). It reports no original participant data: "This article does not contain any studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors."
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The text discusses only tinnitus questionnaires (THI, TQ, TRQ, TSI, THQ, TSQ, TFI) and HADS. Misophonia appears only in the title of a cited reference (ref 198, "Tinnitus, hyperacusis, and misophonia toolbox").
codes.note: This is a guideline/review document with no empirical data, so it is E4_design. It is also essentially not about misophonia: the only mention is in reference 198's title. The cited hyperacusis prevalence in tinnitus (40–86%) comes from secondary sources and is not about misophonia.

codes.sample: 116 low-risk obstetric mothers from the University Hospital of Fuenlabrada, Madrid, Spain. 287 were assessed in the first trimester and 116 again four months after delivery.
codes.instruments: CAE avoidance coping subscale; Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS); Mother and Baby Scales (MABS). None of these measures misophonia.
codes.note: This study looks at postpartum depression, avoidant coping and mother–infant relationships. Misophonia, sound sensitivity and sound intolerance are never mentioned or measured, so there are no misophonia case definitions or counts.

codes.sample: 23 right-handed adults with normal hearing were recruited for an fMRI study. 6 were excluded for head movement, leaving 17 aged 18–34 who were selected by a discrimination screening test.
codes.instruments: None related to misophonia. Edinburgh handedness questionnaire, audiogram, and behavioural same/different discrimination tasks during fMRI.
codes.note: This is an fMRI study of how the brain identifies sound sources (action vs. material of tapping and scraping sounds). Misophonia, sound sensitivity and any misophonia measure are never mentioned. The full text was available. The PDF is dated 2018 (Cerebral Cortex 28:805–818, advance access January 2017), not 2016 as listed.

codes.sample: No human participants. This is an engineering and materials-science study of tunable Schwarz P-type TPMS acoustic metamaterials and lichen meta-foams for reducing environmental noise.
codes.instruments: None. Only acoustic simulations (COMSOL/FEM), sound reduction index measurements, thermogravimetric analysis and flame tests were used.
codes.note: Misophonia appears only once, in the Introduction, as a cited possible effect of environmental noise: "hyperacusis,[15] hearing loss,[16,17,18] misophonia,[19,20] and headaches". There is no misophonia measure, no human sample and no prevalence data.

codes.sample: Three pupillometry experiments with university students/participants: Exp 1 n=22 (17 female), Exp 2 n=22 (15 female), Exp 3 n=22 female (11 passive, 11 active viewing).
codes.instruments: None related to misophonia; Tobii X2-60 eye tracker pupillometry in response to IAPS fear and neutral images.
codes.note: This study looks at how the pupil responds to emotional (fear) versus neutral pictures, testing image duration, habituation and viewing mode. It never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or any auditory measure. Full text was available.

codes.sample: 310 Spanish patients with definite Meniere disease from the MD Consortium who had exome sequencing; 75 were classified as having severe tinnitus (THI > 68, the third quartile) and 235 as having non-severe tinnitus.
codes.instruments: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) and pure-tone audiometry. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This is a genetic study of structural variants in Meniere disease patients with severe tinnitus. The full text never mentions misophonia. Hyperacusis appears only as background in the Discussion. E2_no_misophonia_measure could also apply, but the report is not about misophonia at all.

codes.sample: 44 people with multiple sclerosis (Teruel, Spain; ATUEM/EME members) and 24 caregivers, surveyed June–July 2020 after COVID-19 confinement.
codes.instruments: SF-36, Self-Compassion Scale (SCS/SCS-SF), Compassion Scale (CS), Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS), ad hoc COVID-19 confinement/fears survey. No misophonia measure.
codes.note: This study is about COVID-19 confinement, self-compassion, fatigue and health in people with MS and their caregivers. The full text never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or sound intolerance.

codes.sample: No participant sample. This is a narrative review of animal and human studies on central gain enhancement in tinnitus and hyperacusis.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia measure is used; the text never mentions misophonia.
codes.note: Abstract: "This review will examine the evidence for gain enhancement in the central auditory system in response to cochlear damage." The paper is a review with no primary data, and it covers only tinnitus and hyperacusis, not misophonia. E4_design is listed first in the order of reasons; not_misophonia would also apply.

codes.sample: Exp 1: 100 'Trusted' online participants (auditory research colleagues); Exp 2: 100 Prolific online participants; Exp 3: 42 'Trusted' participants. All adults without known hearing problems.
codes.instruments: No misophonia measure. Only headphone screening tests were used: Huggins Pitch (HP), Anti-Phase (AP; Woods et al., 2017) and Beat Test (BT).
codes.note: The full text is a methods paper that validates online headphone screening tests based on dichotic pitch. It never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or any sound-tolerance measure. The 'pass rates' it reports are about headphone vs loudspeaker detection, not misophonia cases.

codes.sample: 506 first-year full-time students at a large Midwestern US university (Fall 2023); 194 first-generation, 312 continuing-generation.
codes.instruments: University-designed New Student Survey and First-Year Transition Student Survey (financial stress, belonging, commitment, grit, etc.). No misophonia measure.
codes.note: This study looks at what predicts retention and GPA for first-generation and continuing-generation college students. The only link to misophonia is one citation (Vitoratou et al., 2022, an S-Five paper), used only to back up the fit-index thresholds. No misophonia data were collected.

codes.sample: None. This is a scoping review of 39 published studies on tinnitus and decreased sound tolerance in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). It reports no primary data.
codes.instruments: None. The review uses no instrument of its own. Misophonia appears only in the search terms and as part of the umbrella term decreased sound tolerance (DST).
codes.note: The text calls itself a scoping review and says "No primary data were used in the production of this manuscript." The prevalence figures it quotes are second-hand and cover hyperacusis, auditory hypersensitivity or DST, not misophonia specifically. The reference list could be checked for primary studies that measure misophonia.

codes.sample: 284 self-identified ASMR adults recruited via Reddit r/ASMR and 279 age/gender-matched Qualtrics Panel controls (Canada, University of Winnipeg).
codes.instruments: Big Five Inventory (BFI); self-created ASMR Checklist (intensity ratings for 14 stimuli). No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This study is about ASMR and personality, not misophonia. Misophonia comes up only once, in passing, citing Barratt and Davis (2015): "mouth sounds" may trigger "sensations related to misophonia (hatred of specific sounds)". The study used no misophonia measure and reports no misophonia counts. The ASMR group was also recruited through an ASMR forum.

codes.sample: Retrospective clinic records of 78 children aged 2-7 years (58 male, 20 female) in the Northeastern USA, selected because of SPD symptoms on the Sensory Profile and having no other neurodevelopmental or mental disorder.
codes.instruments: Sensory Profile / Sensory Profile-2 (Dunn, 2014), rescored into Miller et al. SPD types; CBCL; VABS-2. No misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.note: The word misophonia never appears in the report. It only measures sensory over-responsivity and auditory processing problems (e.g., auditory 70.6%) with the Sensory Profile, and has no misophonia case definition. The sample was also selected for SPD. 'not_misophonia' would also fit, but E2 comes first in the order of exclusion reasons.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a scoping review of 42 studies on hyperacusis prevalence (34,796 subjects in total across the included studies).
codes.instruments: None. The review summarises hyperacusis measures from the included studies (LDL/ULL, Hyperacusis Questionnaire, NSS, single questions). No misophonia-specific instrument is used.
codes.note: Scoping review ("a scoping review based on the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O'Malley"). 'Misophonia' was only a search term. It reports no misophonia prevalence data; everything is about hyperacusis, so E2 would also apply. Its reference list could be checked for primary studies.

codes.sample: 60 college students in Kerala and Karnataka, India, aged 18–25 (43 female, 17 male), recruited by convenience sampling. They were randomly assigned to watch an ASMR video (n=30) or a neutral video (n=30).
codes.instruments: Smith Relaxation States Inventory (SRSI) and Smith Relaxation Posttest Inventory (SRPI) to measure the outcomes, and the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ) for screening. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This is an experiment on how ASMR videos affect relaxation. Misophonia comes up only once, in the Discussion (p. 8), when citing McErlean & Banissy 2018: "the sensation of ASMR is also associated with a condition called misophonia". Misophonia was not measured, so no counts exist. E2_no_misophonia_measure would be a fair alternative reason, but no sound-tolerance construct was measured either.

codes.sample: 10 experimental houses (5 traditional, 5 modified) in Nampula district, Mozambique; 13 community volunteers (595 sleep-interviews) and 10 construction workers surveyed.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. Ad hoc comfort questionnaire (temperature, sweating, breathing, noise intensity from mosquito buzzing; house rating 1–5).
codes.note: This is a malaria vector-control study of modified houses. The only sound-related measure is volunteers' rating of mosquito buzzing noise intensity as a comfort factor. Misophonia and sound intolerance are not assessed.

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical/methodological paper on open-science practices for ASMR research and reports no empirical sample. The 250-participant example is explicitly hypothetical.
codes.instruments: None used. Misophonia appears only in a cited reference title (McErlean & Banissy, 2018).
codes.note: The paper describes itself as theoretical: "This article is a theoretical article that was not pre-registered nor had data or materials to share." Its topic is ASMR, not misophonia, so not_misophonia would also apply, but E4_design comes first in the order.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a theoretical overview paper on functionalist approaches to emotion.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia measure is used, and misophonia or sound sensitivity is never mentioned.
codes.possible_duplicate: The acknowledgements say a similar version appears in the Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development. This doesn't matter for this review.
codes.note: This is a purely theoretical paper based on an invited address (Campos et al., 1994) about emotion theory. It contains no data and does not mention misophonia. E4_design is the first reason in the list that applies, but not_misophonia would also apply.

codes.sample: 91 participants recruited at and around Utrecht University (posters, flyers, social media, mailing lists): 63 female, 28 male, mean age 25 (range 18-60). They were grouped by self-reported ASMR (37 ASMR, 35 non-ASMR, 19 unsure). The final analysed sample was 82.
codes.instruments: Eye tracker (SMI Hi-Speed) measuring pupil diameter, button presses for tingles, and a self-classification question on ASMR. The full text describes no misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This is an ASMR eye-tracking experiment. Misophonia appears only in the Introduction, citing other studies. No misophonia measure or case definition is reported. The S1 Appendix questionnaire responses were not retrieved; the main text describes them only as demographics, video experience and ASMR experience.

codes.sample: 16 right-ear tinnitus patients with normal hearing from otorhinolaryngology outpatient clinics (Guangzhou, China) and 15 healthy controls from Jinan University staff; resting-state fMRI case-control study.
codes.instruments: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (Chinese), Self-Rating Depression Scale, Self-Rating Anxiety Scale, pure-tone audiometry. No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This is a resting-state fMRI study of tinnitus. The word misophonia never appears and misophonia is not assessed. Hyperacusis appears only as an exclusion criterion ("hyperacousia"). The reason could also be E2, but not_misophonia fits best because sound tolerance was not measured at all.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative review of behavioural, neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies of voice processing in schizophrenia patients with and without auditory verbal hallucinations (AVH).
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia instrument is used or mentioned. The reviewed studies used schizophrenia symptom scales such as SAPS, PANSS and PSYRATS.
codes.note: Page 1 labels the article "REVIEW" and the abstract says "In this review, we consider behavioral, neuroimaging, and electrophysiological data". The paper is also not about misophonia at all; it covers AVH and voice processing in schizophrenia. E4_design is the primary reason because it comes first in the order; not_misophonia also applies.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative review of published studies on sleep, mental health and COVID-19. It reports no primary sample.
codes.instruments: None related to misophonia. The review only discusses sleep measures (e.g., PSQI, RCSQ, SRSS, actigraphy, PSG).
codes.note: The Methods say: "we structured this paper as a narrative review". The paper is also not about misophonia at all: misophonia, sound sensitivity and sound-tolerance measures are never mentioned. E4_design is listed as the primary reason because it comes first in the exclusion order; not_misophonia also applies.

codes.sample: None of its own: this is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies of sensory processing (exteroception and interoception) in people aged 15 or older with interview-diagnosed eating disorders, and in healthy controls.
codes.instruments: Instruments in the reviewed studies: Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile, Sensory Responsiveness Questionnaire, EDI-2 interoceptive awareness subscale, EDI-3 interoceptive deficits subscale, and MAIA. None is specific to misophonia.
codes.possible_duplicate: None
codes.note: This is a review with no original data. Misophonia comes up only once, in the clinical implications section (p.18): "those with a heightened sensitivity to sounds, for example, hyperacusis or misophonia, may benefit from eating in quiet environments". No misophonia measure is used and no misophonia counts are given. The Sensory Responsiveness Questionnaire auditory subscale results are means only.

codes.sample: 257 children aged 6-11 years (49% girls), rated by their female primary caregivers recruited via Prolific (mostly UK). The last 20% were recruited through an extra filter for parents with autism or self-identified autism. 12.8% of the children had diagnosed autism.
codes.instruments: AQ-Child; Glasgow Sensory Questionnaire, parent version (GSQ-P, 7 modality subscales including auditory); DCDQ'07; Spence Children's Anxiety Scale, parent version. None of these is a misophonia instrument.
codes.note: The report does not mention misophonia. Auditory symptoms were measured only with the general GSQ-P auditory subscale (covering aversion, seeking and speech perception), reported as means and SSVS/regression results. There is no misophonia-specific measure or case definition. The only prevalence-type figure is AQ ≥76 (21%), which is about autism.

codes.sample: Online Prolific adults from the US (n = 502 completed everything; 1,041 had questionnaire data) and in-person adults with clinically confirmed ASD from the Seaver Autism Center (n = 56 in the final sample). High-trait and low-trait groups were matched for age and sex (n = 56 each).
codes.instruments: Measures were the BAPQ (autistic traits), the LSAS avoidance items, the AvPD-IS and the ADOS-2 Module 4. No misophonia or sound-sensitivity measure was used.
codes.possible_duplicate: The europepmc text appears to be a preprint version, titled 'Phenotypical divergence between self-reported and clinically ascertained autism', of the Nature Mental Health 2025 article.
codes.note: The study compares online adults with self-reported high autistic traits against adults with clinically ascertained autism, using social anxiety/avoidance measures and social decision-making tasks. The full text never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or auditory symptoms. The 'top 15%' cut-off is on BAPQ autistic-trait scores, not on any misophonia measure.

codes.sample: 138 Polish adults recruited via a social-media link (Google Forms). 63% female, 52.2% aged 18–26. They rated 24 recorded mindfulness-instruction clips (Table 1, p.4).
codes.instruments: No misophonia instrument. The only measures were 5-point Likert ratings of recordings that varied in form, pace, whispering and number of artifacts, plus open-ended comments.
codes.note: This is a study of preferences for mindfulness recordings. Misophonia comes up only in the background and discussion, and in a qualitative remark that some respondents said the recordings 'could be uncomfortable for people with misophonia' (p.11). No misophonia measure, case definition or count is reported. E2_no_misophonia_measure could serve as an alternative reason.

codes.sample: 41 new and existing tinnitus patients from three tinnitus care services in England, interviewed face to face (17 female, 24 male; mostly over 50).
codes.instruments: Semi-structured qualitative interviews (topic guide on tinnitus help-seeking, decision making, information and preferences), analysed with grounded theory. No misophonia measure.
codes.note: This is a qualitative grounded-theory study of what tinnitus patients prefer in outcomes and treatment, and it reports no misophonia counts. The full text never mentions misophonia, so it also fits not_misophonia (and E2, since no misophonia measure is used). E4_design is the primary reason because it comes first in the exclusion order.

codes.sample: Busselton Healthy Ageing Study (Western Australia): population-based cohort of 5,107 non-institutionalized adults aged 45-70, randomly drawn from the electoral roll (2010-2015).
codes.instruments: A single yes/no item for hyperacusis: "Do you consider yourself sensitive or intolerant to everyday sounds", plus follow-up items on sound types, effect on daily life and emotional reactions. No misophonia-specific instrument was used.
codes.note: General sound-sensitivity item framed as hyperacusis: 775/5,107 (15.2%). There is no misophonia-specific case definition. The authors say only that the item "may also capture individuals with ... misophonia". No counts per sound type (paper, talk, etc.) are reported.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a meta-analysis of 192 general-population studies (n = 708,561) on age at onset of ICD/DSM mental disorders.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The pooled studies used ICD/DSM criteria or validated psychometric cut-offs for other mental disorders.
codes.note: This is a systematic review and meta-analysis ("PRISMA/MOOSE-compliant systematic review with meta-analysis"), so E4_design applies. It also doesn't mention misophonia or sound sensitivity anywhere, so not_misophonia would apply too, but E4 comes first in the order. It reports no misophonia counts.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative review of the mechanisms of aminoglycoside ototoxicity and possible ways to prevent it. It reports no primary participant sample.
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia is not measured or mentioned anywhere in the text.
codes.note: The report is about aminoglycoside-related sensorineural hearing loss, not misophonia. It is also a review ("In this article, we review the latest findings...") and would fail E4_design too, but not_misophonia is the main reason. The only prevalence figures are cited estimates of ototoxicity (2%–25% hearing deficits), not misophonia.

codes.sample: 71 healthy adults (34 men, 37 women, aged 19–51) in an M/EEG study in Helsinki. They were not recruited for misophonia. 71 had usable MEG recordings and 66 had usable EEG recordings.
codes.instruments: Weinstein's Noise Sensitivity Scale (21 items) and HADS (depression subscale). No misophonia-specific instrument was used.
codes.possible_duplicate: The study belongs to the 'Tunteet' research protocol, and the questionnaire was part of the HIMAB inventory. Other Kliuchko et al. reports may use the same participants, but none of them is about misophonia.
codes.note: The study measured only general noise sensitivity (Weinstein NSS) and split the sample into tertiles (low N=23, medium N=23, high N=25). Misophonia is never mentioned or measured, so there is no misophonia case definition. The report could also be classed as not_misophonia.

codes.sample: 3,140 Chinese college students (convenience online survey, May–June 2025, 22 provinces); aged 18–27.
codes.instruments: PARS-3 (physical activity), Positive Mental Health Scale, PHQ-9 (depressive symptoms). There is no misophonia or sound-sensitivity measure.
codes.note: This study is about physical activity, positive mental health and depressive symptoms. The full text never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or sound tolerance. The only prevalence it reports is for depression (PHQ-9 ≥ 11: 604 of 3,140, 19.24%), which is not relevant to this review.

codes.sample: Study 1: 804 Spanish adult internet volunteers; Study 2: 605 University of Barcelona students; Study 3: 252 mainly European/North American internet volunteers (Studies 2+3 pooled n=857).
codes.instruments: Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ), BIS/BAS scales, Physical Anhedonia Scale (PAS), NEO-PI-R Openness. No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This paper develops a questionnaire on music reward. It reports 5.5–5.6% with possible musical anhedonia (BMRQ below -1.5 SD with normal PAS; Figure 3), but that measures loss of pleasure from music, not misophonia. Misophonia and sound sensitivity are never mentioned. Here BMRQ is the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire, not the misophonia BMQ-R.

codes.sample: 503 international undergraduate students in the US with valid responses (614 surveyed; 136 male, 367 female), recruited by convenience sampling through the QuestionPro panel.
codes.instruments: Demographic questionnaire, Mathematics Self-Efficacy and Anxiety Questionnaire (MSEAQ; May, 2009) and Core Flow Scale (Martin & Jackson, 2008). No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This is a doctoral dissertation on flow, math self-efficacy and math anxiety. Misophonia comes up only in the Chapter 5 recommendations ('Students with Exceptionalities', p. 147), which cite Cecilione et al. 2022: 'misophonia exists in about 15% of people'. That is a cited figure, not data from this study. Misophonia was never measured in the sample.

codes.sample: None of its own. This is a systematic review of 16 studies (total 5137 participants) on subjective cognitive complaints and executive functions in middle-aged and older adults.
codes.instruments: None related to misophonia. The reviewed studies used neuropsychological tests (MMSE, TMT, Stroop, BRIEF-A, fluency tests, WAIS digits).
codes.note: This is a systematic review ("The present systematic review analyzes the empirical data..."), so it is excluded as E4_design, the first reason in the order. It is also not about misophonia: the topic is subjective cognitive complaints and executive function before dementia. Misophonia and sound sensitivity are never mentioned. The full text was available.

codes.sample: University students and snowball sample (N=63 recruited; final N=40: 20 ASMR experiencers, 20 controls), UK (Bath Spa University).
codes.instruments: ASMR trigger checklist; algometer pain threshold; VAS pain ratings; tingle frequency scale. No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This is an experimental study of how ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response) affects pain. Misophonia is never mentioned, measured or reported. The only classification is ASMR experiencer vs control, based on a trigger checklist.

codes.sample: 1,382 introductory psychology students at a large Midwestern US university; final sample 1,068 after attention-check exclusions (74.9% female, age 18–31).
codes.instruments: PHSS (help-seeking), CMNI-30 (masculine norms), CIPS (imposter phenomenon), Growth Mindset Scale, R-SPQ-2F (study approaches); no misophonia or sound-tolerance measure.
codes.note: This study is about masculine ideology, imposter phenomenon, mindset, study habits, help-seeking and academic outcomes in college students. Misophonia and sound sensitivity are not mentioned anywhere in the full text, so the report is irrelevant to the review.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a scoping review of 21 records on hyperacusis in children (under 18).
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The included studies assessed hyperacusis using ULLs, semi-structured interviews, questionnaires (e.g., Sensory Profile Short Form, Williams Syndrome Questionnaire), a VAS, observation and tuning-fork neurological assessment.
codes.note: Scoping review (Methods: 'a scoping review was determined to be the most suitable methodology'). It is about hyperacusis, not misophonia; records on misophonia without hyperacusis were explicitly excluded. It reports no misophonia prevalence data. A secondary reason would be E2 / not_misophonia.

codes.sample: Three Finnish university students at the University of Lapland, aged 26–27 (2 male, 1 female), who identified as ASMR experiencers. They were purposively sampled and interviewed by email and Skype between December 2019 and March 2020.
codes.instruments: Semi-structured qualitative interviews (10 questions based on the PERMA well-being model), analysed with interpretative phenomenological analysis. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This is a qualitative IPA study of ASMR and well-being with no counts, so it is excluded for design (E4). Misophonia comes up only in the introduction, as a citation of other studies (Rouw & Erfanian 2018; McErlean & Banissy 2018). The paper does not measure misophonia, so E2 and not_misophonia would also apply. The sample was also selected for ASMR experience.

codes.sample: 50 adult day-surgery patients at Sydney Adventist Hospital, Australia (55 approached), randomised to an ASMR video (n=25) or a control educational video (n=25).
codes.instruments: STAI (state and trait), Visual Analogue Anxiety Scale (VAAS), Amsterdam Pre-operative Anxiety and Information Scale (APAIS), and vital signs. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This is an RCT on whether ASMR reduces pre-operative anxiety. Misophonia comes up only in the title of a cited reference (ref 20, Janik McErlean & Banissy 2018). Misophonia was not assessed and no misophonia counts are reported. The only case counts are for anxiety cut-offs (VAAS >46, APAIS >11).

codes.sample: 38 Dutch undergraduate psychology students (33 female, 5 male; aged 17-35, mean 20.42) at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, recruited through the SONA subject pool and not selected for ASMR experience.
codes.instruments: An adapted ASMR checklist (Barratt & Davis 2015), POMS, the Flanker task, HEXACO-SPI, heart rate, EDA and EEG. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This study is about ASMR, not misophonia. Misophonia comes up only once, in the Introduction, as background: a citation of Janik McErlean & Banissy 2018, who used the MQ. Misophonia was not measured in this sample. The only prevalence-type figure is ASMR tingles: 15 of 38 participants (37%). Arguably 'not_misophonia' would fit too, but E2 is listed first in the reason order.

codes.sample: No misophonia sample. This is a statistics methods paper. Its only data examples are reanalysed t values from other studies (e.g., N = 80 in Grider & Malmberg, 2008; 48 police officers in Plant & Peruche, 2005).
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia or sound-sensitivity measure is used.
codes.note: Rouder et al. (2009) is a methods paper on JZS Bayes factor t tests. It does not mention misophonia at all. It was probably retrieved because misophonia studies cite it for their statistics. It could also be classed as E4_design (a theoretical paper), but not_misophonia applies more directly.

codes.sample: None. This is an editorial summarising a Frontiers research topic on tinnitus heterogeneity and reports no original data.
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia comes up only once, in a summary of Palumbo et al.
codes.note: This is an editorial with no original data. The only mention of misophonia is in the Chapter 3 section: "Reaction to external sounds, such as misophonia—the dislike of sound, also contributes to the heterogeneity of the tinnitus population (Palumbo et al.)." It gives no prevalence counts. The cited Palumbo et al. paper (Front Aging Neurosci 2018) could be checked separately.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative review of the sensory processing literature in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), covering symptom and neuroscience studies.
codes.instruments: None administered. It reviews general sensory questionnaires (Sensory Profile, SEQ, SensOR, Sensory Perception Quotient) and EEG/fMRI/MEG studies. No misophonia-specific instrument is used.
codes.note: The paper describes itself as a review: "The purpose of this paper is to integrate the empirical literature on sensory processing in ASD from the last decade". It never mentions misophonia, so it also fails E2 and could count as not_misophonia. E4_design is the first exclusion reason that applies in the specified order.

codes.sample: 213 Swedish youth aged 7–18 years: 85 with OCD and 82 with anxiety disorders (treatment-seeking, child and adolescent mental health unit), plus 46 non-clinical comparison youth recruited from local schools, 2015–2019.
codes.instruments: Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile (Dunn & Brown, 2002); OCI-CV; SCARED; CDI-S; CY-BOCS; MINI-KID. No misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.note: Misophonia is never mentioned. The only sound-related data come from general sensory-processing quadrants (low registration, sensory sensitivity, sensation avoiding), classified as >1 SD above the norm. These are general sensory over-responsivity measures, not misophonia case definitions. 'not_misophonia' would also fit.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative review of autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) and contains no original data.
codes.instruments: None used. The review mentions the Misophonia Questionnaire only when citing another study (Janik McErlean & Banissy 2018).
codes.note: The report is labelled "REVIEW" (p.1). Misophonia comes up only in the section on what ASMR is not (p.2), which cites ref 4, Janik McErlean & Banissy 2018, PeerJ 6:e5351. That study is a possible source to screen separately; its ASMR sample may be self-selected.

codes.sample: 1024 Chinese college students (613 female, 411 male), aged 16–23, convenience sample from Anhui Province, surveyed online Sept–Nov 2023.
codes.instruments: AQ (Autism-Spectrum Quotient), IERQ, Social Self-Efficacy scale, CES-D. No misophonia or sound-sensitivity measure.
codes.note: The study looks at autistic traits, interpersonal emotion regulation, social self-efficacy and depression. Misophonia, sound sensitivity and sound tolerance are never mentioned anywhere in the full text.

codes.sample: The retrieved text describes 47 healthy adult university volunteers (32 female, aged 19-53), screened online with the ASRS into Hi and Lo ADHD-trait groups. This is a different study from the one in the report title.
codes.instruments: Retrieved text: ASRS (ADHD self-report), plus simultaneity judgement and temporal order judgement tasks. It contains no misophonia instrument. The instruments of the titled paper cannot be checked from this text.
codes.possible_duplicate: The retrieved text is by the same authors (Panagiotidi, Overton, Stafford). It refers to their unpublished general-population ASRS scoping sample of 800 people, which may overlap with the titled paper's sample.
codes.note: Wrong full text retrieved. Title: "The relationship between ADHD traits and sensory sensitivity in the general population". Text: "Multisensory integration and ADHD-like traits..." by the same authors. Neither mentions misophonia, so the right paper is probably E2_no_misophonia_measure. Check the correct full text.

codes.sample: Parents of 601 children aged 6–11 from 22 state schools in southern England (MULTISENSE cohort; all 3690 parents invited). 32 SEND, 510 typically developing, 62 SEND status unknown.
codes.instruments: Parent-completed Glasgow Sensory Questionnaire (GSQ-P, 42 items) and its reduced form (rGSQ-P, 24 items), SDQ, SCARED, EQ-C. The study used no misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.possible_duplicate: Cites Simner, Rinaldi, Koursarou & Ward (2022, J Autism Dev Disord), which used the Sussex Misophonia Scale for Adolescents alongside the GSQ-P/rGSQ-P. That report may draw on a related cohort and should be screened separately.
codes.note: Only general sensory hyper/hypo-sensitivity is measured. Misophonia appears only where the authors cite earlier validity work against the Sussex Misophonia Scale (Simner et al., 2022). This sample had no misophonia measure or case definition. The only sound items are general (e.g., 'dislike loud noises?'). Results are means, alphas and correlations only.

codes.sample: None. This is a methods guideline (IHS Clinical Trials Standing Committee, 4th edition) on how to run controlled trials of acute migraine treatment. No participants were recruited and no data were collected.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The only sound-related item is migraine-associated phonophobia, recorded as present or absent or on a 4-point severity scale. This is a recommendation, not a measurement.
codes.possible_duplicate: None. It replaces the 3rd edition (2012) of the IHS guidelines, but none of the editions report misophonia data.
codes.note: This is a consensus guideline with no empirical data, so E4_design is the first exclusion reason that applies. It is also not about misophonia (not_misophonia would apply as well): the word misophonia never appears, and phonophobia is mentioned only as a migraine-associated symptom and trial endpoint. The full text was available, so the decision is not 'unclear'.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a systematic review of 5 experimental studies on soundscape psychophysiology, with participants who were mostly university students.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The reviewed studies used physiological measures (HR, HRV, SCL, RR, EMG) and perceptual ratings of soundscapes (pleasantness, arousal, eventfulness).
codes.note: A systematic review of soundscape psychophysiology. It does not mention misophonia anywhere and reports no primary data or misophonia counts. It is excluded as a review (E4_design); it would also fit not_misophonia.

codes.sample: 12 paid adult participants (8 male, 4 female; mean age 29, SD 4.6) in a laboratory experiment rating the dissimilarity of 12 IADS sounds.
codes.instruments: Self-Assessment Manikin ratings of valence and arousal; dissimilarity ratings analysed with INDSCAL multidimensional scaling. No measure of misophonia.
codes.note: This is an experimental study of how emotions induced by sounds shape the way people categorise everyday sounds. The full text never mentions misophonia, uses no misophonia instrument and reports no case counts.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative review of cortical hyperexcitability in autism spectrum disorders. It briefly cites the authors' earlier work on visually evoked responses in ASD vs TD participants.
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia is never assessed or mentioned. Sensory measures discussed are EEG/fMRI/MRS/TMS and psychophysical tasks.
codes.note: The abstract calls the paper a review ("this review illustrates..."). It does not mention misophonia at all; it covers only general sensory hypersensitivity in ASD, so not_misophonia would also apply. E4_design is listed first in the order, so it is the primary reason.

codes.sample: 101 adults with tinnitus pooled from four earlier neuroimaging studies at UMCG (2004–2019). 35 had clinically normal hearing (NHT) and 66 had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (HLT). This is a retrospective case-control study.
codes.instruments: Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ, 14 items, cut-off ≥22), Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI), and pure-tone audiometry. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.possible_duplicate: The data come from four earlier UMCG studies (refs 17–20). The HLT sample probably overlaps with the authors' earlier VBM study of hyperacusis (ref 14).
codes.note: Only hyperacusis was measured (HQ ≥22: 22/35 in NHT and 25/66 in HLT). Misophonia comes up only in the Discussion, where earlier fMRI studies are cited ("participants with misophonia... showed increased SMA activity"). There is no misophonia-specific measure and no misophonia case count.

codes.sample: Adults aged 18–35 recruited after routine vision exams. Preliminary experiment n = 97; Exp 1 n = 70; Exp 2 n = 46; Exp 3 n = 36 (some participants overlap). Overall 106 males and 111 females.
codes.instruments: Visual discomfort rating scale (0–5) for striped gratings, plus pupillometry with a Tobii 4C eye tracker. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This study is about visual discomfort from striped patterns (pattern glare) and pupil responses. Misophonia appears only once, in a Discussion citation of Qiu et al. (2025): "misophonic visual cues generally elicit constriction, this response was attenuated in the misophonic group." No misophonia measure or prevalence data. The high-VD group (n=20 of 42) is about visual discomfort, not misophonia.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a narrative review of neuromodulators in depression, schizophrenia, anxiety, ASD and AUD.
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia is not mentioned or measured.
codes.note: Narrative review from the ISN/JNC Flagship School ('In this review, which originated from the International Society for Neurochemistry...'). It has no primary data and does not mention misophonia. E4_design comes first in the exclusion order; not_misophonia would also apply.

codes.sample: 264 adults with tinnitus (158 male, 106 female; mean age 58.7, range 24-85) pooled retrospectively from tinnitus research studies at NIHR Nottingham Hearing BRU / MRC IHR, 2008-2014.
codes.instruments: Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ, Khalfa et al.), THI, THQ, BDI-II, BDI-FS, BAI, uncomfortable loudness levels (ULLs). No misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.note: The study measured only hyperacusis (HQ >28: 19/264, 7.2%). Misophonia appears only once, in the Introduction, where it is contrasted with hyperacusis. HQ item 14 ('Certain sounds cause stress and irritation') is a general hyperacusis item, not a misophonia case definition. The sample (tinnitus) would otherwise qualify under I1.

codes.sample: No participant sample. The article analyses 64 pages of 'found data' (user comments) from ASMR YouTube videos and Reddit /ASMR threads, taken from Klausen (2016).
codes.instruments: None. The study is a qualitative netnography and theoretical media and sound-studies analysis. Misophonia is not measured.
codes.possible_duplicate: The empirical material comes from Klausen, H.B. (2016), a master's thesis at Aarhus University. It is also qualitative and about ASMR.
codes.note: This is a Danish media-studies article about ASMR, not misophonia. It is a qualitative and theoretical analysis of user comments with no counts. Misophonia appears only in one reference title (McErlean & Banissy, 2018). E4_design is the first exclusion reason in the order. not_misophonia would also apply.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative conference report summarising presentations from the 2025 World Tinnitus Congress / International Tinnitus Seminar (Warsaw). It contains no original misophonia sample.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The report mentions the THI and CTQ for tinnitus, and UCLs for hyperacusis.
codes.note: This is a review or conference summary (labelled 'Hypothesis papers'). It mentions misophonia only in the context of CBT treatment ('CBT is effective in reducing distress for patients experiencing tinnitus, hyperacusis, and misophonia', p.2). It gives no misophonia prevalence counts. The only prevalence figure is for paediatric tinnitus and hyperacusis ('3–6% of children', p.7).

codes.sample: Study 1: 68 patients from a tertiary tinnitus and hyperacusis clinic in Seoul (tinnitus n=15, tinnitus+hearing loss n=12, hyperacusis n=21, normal controls n=20). Study 2: 100 tinnitus patients who used sound generators (tinnitus only n=64, tinnitus+hyperacusis n=36).
codes.instruments: Loudness discomfort levels (pure tone and white-band noise), Hyperacusis Questionnaire (Khalfa), a single sound-sensitivity question, a 0-10 hyperacusis distress rating, VAS tinnitus scores and the THI. No misophonia-specific instrument was used.
codes.note: Misophonia comes up only in the Introduction, as a term to tell apart from hyperacusis ("Misophonia is a developed aversion to sounds such as chewing or breathing"). Only hyperacusis was measured (LDLs and the hyperacusis questionnaire), and no misophonia case definition or count is reported.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a systematic review of studies (2015–2022) on auditory processing in people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
codes.instruments: None. The report does not use or cite any misophonia instrument; the word misophonia does not appear in the text.
codes.note: This is a systematic review following PRISMA ("This systematic review follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines"). It reports no original data and does not address misophonia; it only mentions hyperacusis and auditory hypersensitivity in ASD. It could also be excluded as not_misophonia, but E4_design comes first in the order.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative/theoretical review of the neuroscience behind Ayres Sensory Integration.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia measure is used; the paper only mentions the Sensory Profile and SIPT, citing other studies.
codes.note: The paper describes itself as a review: "This paper reviews the neural foundations of sensory integration and praxis..." (Section 6, Discussion). It never mentions misophonia; it covers only sensory modulation and hyper-/hypo-reactivity in general terms. The not_misophonia reason would also apply, but E4_design comes first in the order of reasons.

codes.sample: 501 social media comments (441 YouTube, 53 Instagram, 7 Ekşi Sözlük) on two Turkish ASMR-containing ads (LC Waikiki, Permolit Paint), collected October 2021 to January 2022. The units are comments, not participants.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. Content analysis of comments using an inductive coding scheme (attitude direction, expressions, reasons, targets, behavioural attitude).
codes.note: This is a marketing study about ASMR in advertising. Misophonia comes up only in the literature review and discussion (e.g., 'may trigger misophonia syndrome for some audiences'). No misophonia instrument, case definition or count is reported. E2_no_misophonia_measure would also be a defensible primary reason.

codes.sample: 529 adults aged 18-73 (320 female, 209 male), Turkey, 2016. 104 were recruited among Marmara University medical students and their friends/families (10 of these had hyperacusis complaints); 425 were recruited via Facebook/Twitter. There were no inclusion criteria apart from age 18 or over.
codes.instruments: Khalfa Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ, Turkish version, 14 items); Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI).
codes.note: Only hyperacusis was measured, using the HQ. Table 4 reports hyperacusis bands, e.g. 'Complete hyperacusis (29 points or higher) | 17 | 3.2', but these are not misophonia. The Discussion mentions that one HQ item ('Do noise and certain sounds cause you stress and irritation?') captures annoyance/misophonia, but there is no misophonia-specific case definition and no item-level counts.

codes.sample: 34 normal-hearing adults (9 females; mean age 26.7) in a lab-based evaluative conditioning experiment (Gothenburg region, Västra Götaland ethics approval).
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. Measures: loudness, fear and threat visual analog scales, 9-point valence/arousal scales, and electrodermal activity.
codes.note: This is an experimental study of how aversive conditioning changes loudness perception of noise bands. It does not mention misophonia, does not use a misophonia measure and does not count cases. A second reason would also apply: it is an experiment with no screened unselected pool.

codes.sample: 216 university students taking a psychology class at a Tokyo university, surveyed 20 Jan–5 Feb 2012. Mean age 20.3 (range 18–27). 101 male, 113 female, 2 other. Not recruited on the basis of sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: Japanese version of Khalfa's Hyperacusis Questionnaire (14 items, adapted to a 6-point scale); HADS; ad hoc yes/no items on medical history and comorbidities.
codes.note: Only hyperacusis was measured, using Khalfa's HQ. Hyperacusis was defined as a score of 40 or more (about the top 5%; 10/216). Misophonia and selective sound sensitivity are never mentioned. HQ items 6 and 14 mention 'specific kinds of sounds', but the scale is a general hyperacusis measure, not a misophonia-specific case definition.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is an edited Turkish textbook on psychiatric nursing with 13 narrative chapters (e.g., psychological first aid, reminiscence therapy, telenursing, ASMR and stress).
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia comes up only in reference titles in Chapter 11 (ASMR), e.g., McErlean & Banissy 2018 and Scofield 2019.
codes.note: This is a narrative textbook or review, not a study with original data. The retrieved text covers only the opening page and reference list of each chapter, but the table of contents shows no chapter on misophonia. Misophonia appears only in cited reference titles in the ASMR chapter (p. 148/ref 6, ref 40). The report is also essentially not about misophonia.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a systematic review of 167 publications on music-evoked chills (MECs), covering 1980 to April 2020.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia instrument is used or reported. The prevalence figures are for music-evoked chills, not misophonia.
codes.note: This is a systematic review of music-evoked chills (Methods: "we systematically review the literature on MECs"), so it fails E4_design. It is also not about misophonia: the term never appears. The only mention of aversive sound reactions is "displeasurable chills can also be experienced in response to unpleasant sounds", which is not a misophonia measure.

codes.sample: 16 adolescents aged 12–17 with an autism diagnosis (12 male, 4 female) from 3 mainstream schools in the East of England. AASP data were analysed for 14 of them. The sample was recruited for autism, not misophonia.
codes.instruments: Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile (AASP; Brown & Dunn 2002a), plus an ad hoc qualitative questionnaire that asks how touch, vision, hearing and smell affect pupils in the classroom (1–10 ratings and open questions). Neither is a misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.possible_duplicate: The footnote says the study was done for a Master's dissertation, so the thesis may describe the same sample.
codes.note: The study covers general sensory processing (AASP quadrants) and hearing difficulties in the classroom. It never mentions misophonia and has no misophonia case definition. A 'scraping sound' quote is not a misophonia measure. The study is not about misophonia, so not_misophonia would also fit; E2 was chosen because it comes first in the rule order.

codes.sample: 34 healthy young adults (17 females, 17 males) in an experiment on postural control. They were enrolled with inclusion criteria of no balance or auditory disorders. No unselected screening pool is reported.
codes.instruments: Hyperacusis Questionnaire (HQ, 15 items, 0–45); a 1–10 rating of how annoying the experimental sounds were (vuvuzela, fork, chainsaw, ambulance, styrofoam, screech, grinder). No misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.note: The study measures only hyperacusis (HQ) and annoyance with generic loud or unpleasant sounds. It does not mention misophonia or use any misophonia case definition. The HQ results are given only as means/SD and as single extreme cases ("highest score... 32 points"; "lowest score, 2 points"), so there is no prevalence count either.

codes.sample: No original human sample. This is a narrative review of sensory (mainly tactile) abnormalities in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and in genetic mouse models of ASD.
codes.instruments: None. The paper does not use any misophonia instrument. It only mentions general sensory measures from the studies it reviews (Short Sensory Profile, Sensory Profile, Sensory Experiences Questionnaire, Tactile Defensiveness and Discrimination Test-Revised).
codes.note: The paper calls itself a review ("In this review, we will address the neurobiological bases of sensory processing in ASD"). It does not mention misophonia anywhere. Its only hearing content is auditory processing in ASD. So it is also 'not_misophonia', but E4_design comes first in the order of exclusion reasons. It reports no prevalence counts.

codes.sample: 30 healthy Japanese young adults (15 male, 15 female, mean age 20.8 ± 0.5) who had watched ASMR videos but never experienced tingling; fMRI experiment.
codes.instruments: fMRI; post-scan Likert (1-5) mood questionnaire covering "relaxed mood" and "tingling mood". No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: This is an fMRI study of ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response). Misophonia comes up only once, in the Discussion, as a citation: "Right insular activation has been reported in misophonia... (Schröder et al., 2019)". Misophonia was not measured and no counts are reported. If the reviewer considers the topic misophonia-adjacent, the fallback reason would be E2_no_misophonia_measure.

codes.sample: 111 adults with confirmed Tourette syndrome were recruited from the Tourette syndrome specialty clinic at Hannover Medical School (mean age 34.8, 37 female).
codes.instruments: PUTS9, NJRE-QR, USP-SPS, YGTSS, ATQ, GTS-QoL, Y-BOCS, OC-TCDQ-R, FSU-12, BDI-II, BAI. None of these is a misophonia instrument.
codes.possible_duplicate: Most patients were also in the Online-Tics and Canna-Tics studies (refs 20 and 21). This doesn't matter here because the report contains no misophonia data.
codes.note: The study looks at non-just-right experiences, premonitory urges, tics and OCD in Tourette patients. Misophonia, sound sensitivity and decreased sound tolerance are never mentioned or measured. The USP-SPS measures general sensory phenomena, not misophonia. The only counts given are for OCD (Y-BOCS ≥16, n=13), depression (n=22) and anxiety (n=33).

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a narrative review of medical screening tests (LDCT for lung cancer, PSA, mammography) that uses a hypothetical numerical example of 10,000 subjects.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia instrument is used or mentioned.
codes.possible_duplicate: None.
codes.note: This is a methods review in Inhalation Toxicology about screening test sensitivity, specificity, PPV and ROC curves. Misophonia, sound sensitivity and hearing are never mentioned. It would also fall under E4_design, but not_misophonia is the main reason. The full text was retrieved and checked.

codes.sample: Delphi panel on ASMR research priorities. Phase 1: 98 participants from 22 countries (59 academic researchers, 23 ASMR creators, 14 audience or community members, 2 other). Phase 2: 69 participants (52 researchers, 17 non-researchers). Phase 3: at least 26 attendees.
codes.instruments: No misophonia instrument was given to anyone. The Delphi used open-ended suggestions for research priorities, thematic analysis, and best/worst scaling votes (bwsTools). Misophonia is mentioned only in background text and in one research-priority area (Area 7).
codes.note: Expert-consensus (Delphi) study setting ASMR research priorities, not misophonia. Misophonia appears only in the introduction and in Table 1, Area 7 (ASMR and sound intolerance including misophonia). No participant was assessed for misophonia and no counts are given. E4_design could also apply: a consensus or agenda paper with no misophonia data.

codes.sample: 32 adults aged 19–65 with self-reported pain hyperacusis (noxacusis) lasting at least 1 year, recruited by snowball sampling online (lab website, social media, ResearchMatch). 31 answered the comorbidity questions.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc self-report checklist of co-morbid conditions that included a 'Misophonia' item (self-reported condition). No validated misophonia instrument was used.

case_definitions.definition: Self-reported co-morbid misophonia (item on a comorbid conditions checklist)
case_definitions.quote: Thirty-one participants responded to the audiovestibular, neurological, and mental health questions. ... Misophonia | 16.13% (n = 5)

codes.note: Two points to check. (1) Participants were recruited for pain hyperacusis. I1 allows hyperacusis as 'another condition', but E1 mentions sound sensitivity, so confirm this sample fits I1. (2) Misophonia comes only from one self-reported comorbidity checklist item, with no definition or validated tool. If that is not accepted as a misophonia measure, exclude under E2.

codes.sample: Exp 1: 46 Japanese university volunteers (Kobe University) prescreened for prior ASMR experience. Exp 2: 42 volunteers who were not prescreened (27 had experienced ASMR before).
codes.instruments: ASMR Questionnaire (Barratt & Davis), Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ), Adult/Adolescent Sensory Profile (AASP), emBODY body maps, and VAS ratings of ASMR intensity, valence and arousal. No misophonia measure.
codes.note: This is a psychophysical study of ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response). Misophonia is never mentioned, and no misophonia-specific instrument or case definition is used. The only sound-related sensory measure is the AASP. E2_no_misophonia_measure could also apply, but not_misophonia comes first in the order and fits better.

codes.sample: 10 ASMR-sensitive adults (3 female, 7 male, mean age 23.6, range 18–33), recruited via online ASMR forums; 25 initially considered, 18 screened in person, 11 scanned, 10 analysed. Dartmouth College, USA.
codes.instruments: No misophonia measure. ASMR sensitivity was screened by self-report while watching ASMR videos; during fMRI, participants pressed buttons to mark baseline, relaxing and tingling sensations.
codes.possible_duplicate: Funded by a Senior Honors Thesis Grant (Dartmouth College), so a related undergraduate thesis may exist. This doesn't matter, because the report is not eligible.
codes.note: This fMRI study is about ASMR, not misophonia. The word misophonia never appears in the text, and no misophonia instrument or case definition is used. The sample was also selected for ASMR sensitivity through online ASMR forums. Full text was available.

codes.sample: None. This is a methods paper that develops a risk-of-bias tool. It reports no participants and no prevalence data.
codes.instruments: None related to misophonia. The paper describes the ROBINS-I risk-of-bias tool for non-randomised studies of interventions.
codes.note: ROBINS-I is a methods tool for judging risk of bias in non-randomised intervention studies. The paper never mentions misophonia or sound sensitivity, so not_misophonia comes first in the order. It may have been retrieved because the review uses risk-of-bias tools, but it is not a primary study. It is also a methods paper with no data, so E4_design would apply too.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a perspective/review article that brings together genetic, epidemiological, neuroimaging and clinical evidence on tinnitus versus tinnitus disorder.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The tinnitus and mood questionnaires it mentions (TQ, THI, TFI, HADS, BDI) appear only in a proposed grading table.
codes.note: The article calls itself a perspective ("This perspective synthesizes genetic, epidemiological, and neuroimaging evidence..."), with no original data. It also never mentions misophonia, so not_misophonia would apply too; E4_design is listed first, so it is the primary reason.

codes.sample: Parent questionnaire for pupils at one special-needs school in Kanagawa, Japan, who use hearing protectors every day (earmuffs/earplugs): 22 eligible (20 boys, 2 girls; 21 autism, 1 PDD), 15 questionnaires returned. The school had 304 pupils in total, and 7.2% of them used protectors.
codes.instruments: An ad hoc 40-item parent questionnaire on hyperacusis (聴覚過敏): history, current symptoms, disliked sounds, other sensory sensitivities and coping measures. No misophonia-specific instrument or case definition was used.
codes.note: The sample was chosen for daily hearing-protector use, i.e. for sound sensitivity/hyperacusis (E1). E2 also applies: only hyperacusis was measured. Misophonia appears only in the Discussion (p.7–8), as a guess that it 'coexists' with hyperacusis in ASD. The 7.2% protector-use rate in the whole school (304 pupils) is not a misophonia measure.

codes.sample: 282 screened, 266 analysed. Adults familiar and unfamiliar with ASMR, recruited by word of mouth, ASMR social media (e.g., reddit r/ASMR), university advertisements and Prolific. They were recruited for ASMR, not for misophonia or sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: One ad hoc self-report item described as 'pertaining to misophonia': 'Are you made extremely uncomfortable by certain sounds, even if these sounds are quiet? e.g. polystyrene, ceramic, chalk. (0 = no discomfort, 10 = absolute discomfort)'.
codes.possible_duplicate: None found. Not the same sample as McErlean & Banissy (2018, PeerJ), which is cited as earlier work from the same lab on misophonia and ASMR.
codes.note: The 0–10 misophonia item appears only in Methods and briefly in the Discussion ('Here, we used a single question'). No cut-off, distribution, count or proportion is given. Raw data are on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/PAZR5) but not in the report. The item's examples (polystyrene, chalk) are closer to general sound aversion than to typical misophonia triggers.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a theoretical and review paper on atypical resource allocation in autism spectrum conditions.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia instrument is used or mentioned.
codes.possible_duplicate: The paper notes it grew out of the author's UCLA dissertation and says an earlier version of the approach is in Goldknopf (2006). Neither appears to contain misophonia prevalence data.
codes.note: The abstract describes this as a purely theoretical/review paper ("Based on a review of the literature and on reports by people with autism"). The full text never mentions misophonia, and no misophonia prevalence data are reported. It could also be excluded as not_misophonia, but E4_design comes first in the exclusion order.

codes.sample: Online Prolific adults: 246 recruited, 206 analysed for the behavioural task, 173 completed psychometric surveys. 143 more online participants were added for the factor analysis (n = 320).
codes.instruments: STAI-T, Zung Self-rating Depression Scale (SDS), OCI-R. No misophonia instrument.
codes.note: This study is about reward prediction errors, memory and positive affect. It uses a bandit task and a face-recognition task. The full text never mentions misophonia, sound sensitivity or any auditory measure.

codes.sample: 648 Japanese participants: 247 college students and 401 working adults recruited through a temp agency (276 male, 371 female, 1 other; age 18–60).
codes.instruments: Synesthesia questionnaire (Chun and Hupé, 2013), plus a mirror-touch item; ASMR questionnaire and flow-to-ASMR scale (Barratt and Davis, 2015). No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: The study is about ASMR and synesthesia. Misophonia is mentioned only in passing in the Discussion ("eating sounds may trigger ASMR in one context, but misophonia in another"). It was not measured and no misophonia counts are reported. E2 could also apply, but no sound-tolerance construct was measured either, so not_misophonia fits better.

codes.sample: Patients with hyperacusis taking part in a remote counseling program (HAT-Online). The program sample size is not given; only anecdotal reports and mean ratings of the program materials are provided.
codes.instruments: None specific to misophonia. Misophonia is only mentioned as another name for 'annoyance hyperacusis'. The University of Iowa Hyperacusis Questionnaire is cited for background.
codes.note: Clinical focus article that describes how a hyperacusis counseling program was developed. It is descriptive, with no prevalence data. It reports no misophonia measure and no counts. If E4 were not applied, E2 (no misophonia measure) would also apply.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a theoretical/clinical practice paper for child-centred therapists working with autistic children. It includes three first-person sense portraits by autistic authors.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia measure was administered. Misophonia is mentioned only once, in footnote 5 on page 9, which cites Rinaldi et al., 2023.
codes.note: Narrative/practice paper with no data collection. The only mention of misophonia is on page 9, footnote 5: "for some autistic children with profiles indicative of misophonia, elements of these possibilities may prove deregulating (for an overview see, Rinaldi, Simner, Koursarou, & Ward, 2023)". Rinaldi et al. 2023 may itself be worth screening separately.

codes.sample: Residents of four elderly care facilities in northeast China (Harbin, Changchun). 318 surveys before COVID-19 (153 male, 165 female) and 376 after (184 male, 192 female). Residents were included if they had lived there 6 months or more and scored 1–4 on the Rockwood frailty scale.
codes.instruments: Ad hoc 7-point Likert questionnaire on comfort with the dining-room environment (acoustic, lighting, thermal, air quality, odour). Objective measures: sound pressure level, illuminance, luminance, temperature, humidity, CO, CO2, O2. No misophonia instrument.
codes.possible_duplicate: Pre-pandemic physical measurements refer to an earlier joint study, Mu and Kang (2022). This is not relevant to misophonia.
codes.note: The study is about dining-room environmental comfort (acoustic comfort, sound pressure level tolerance, etc.) among elderly care residents before and after COVID-19. It does not mention misophonia or misophonia-like reactions to specific sounds, and no misophonia case definition or counts are reported.

codes.sample: 13 participants with autism (DSM-IV, confirmed with ADI-R) and 13 control participants, adolescents and adults; 31 were recruited for a combined EEG/fMRI study.
codes.instruments: No misophonia instrument. Measures: WAIS-III short form (IQ), Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ), ADI-R, and concurrent EEG/fMRI during a speech documentary.
codes.note: This is a neurophysiology study of theta/gamma cortical oscillations in response to speech in autism. It never mentions misophonia or sound intolerance and assesses neither, so no prevalence data are given. The full text appears complete.

codes.sample: Four naive adult subjects (2 male, 2 female, mean age 26) with normal hearing, University of Florence psychophysics experiment.
codes.instruments: None related to misophonia; multiple object-tracking task with concurrent visual contrast or auditory pitch discrimination tasks.
codes.note: Psychophysics study on whether vision and audition share attentional resources (dual-task paradigm, n=4). The report does not mention misophonia or sound sensitivity, so it gives no prevalence data.

codes.sample: 197 adults (students and alumni in Finland, N=91; psychology students in Italy, N=106), aged 19-56, grouped as nonmusicians (103), amateurs (44) and professional musicians (50). Not recruited for misophonia.
codes.instruments: Weinstein's Noise Sensitivity Scale (21 items); HIMAB music background questions; Seashore pitch/time tests; online MBEA. No misophonia-specific instrument.
codes.note: Only general noise sensitivity was measured (Weinstein scale, total score range 25-121, mean 81.07). Misophonia is never mentioned and there is no misophonia case definition. Results are given only as means, ANOVAs and Spearman correlations.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative (state-of-the-art) review of sensory processing in autism spectrum disorder.
codes.instruments: None. No primary data were collected.
codes.note: Narrative review: "No new data were created or analyzed in this study." It mentions misophonia only in passing, citing ref [136]: "Approximately 50–70% of individuals with ASD exhibit atypical behavioral responses to environmental sounds such as misophonia, phonophobia...". Ref [136] could be checked as a source of primary studies.

codes.sample: 381 patients (170 female, 211 male; mean age 43.9 ± 15.0 years) with a primary complaint of hyperacusis. They attended the London Tinnitus and Hyperacusis Centre between 1979 and 2012. This was a retrospective analysis of clinical records.
codes.instruments: Pure-tone audiometry (hearing thresholds) and loudness discomfort levels (LDLs) from 0.125 to 8 kHz. Hyperacusis was diagnosed from patient history and symptoms. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: Misophonia appears only once, in the Introduction, as another form of decreased sound tolerance ("Other forms of decreased sound tolerance are misophonia (strong dislike of sounds)..."). It was not assessed. The outcomes were hyperacusis/LDL and tinnitus (86% had tinnitus). The clinical sample would qualify, but there is no misophonia-specific measure or case definition.

codes.sample: None. A theoretical and analytical media-studies paper about ASMR role-play videos on YouTube; no participants were sampled.
codes.instruments: None. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.possible_duplicate: None
codes.note: Theoretical/conceptual paper on ASMR (haptic audio-visuality) with no original data. Misophonia comes up only once, in passing (p.5): some people find ASMR videos 'annoying or misophonic' (citing Waldron 2017; McGeoch & Rouw 2020). Also essentially not_misophonia, but E4_design applies first in the order.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a theoretical/review paper on anxiety and sensory over-responsivity in children with ASD.
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia is not assessed. The paper only discusses sensory over-responsivity (SOR) and anxiety measures in general terms.
codes.note: The abstract says: "We propose three possible theories... In this paper, we examine support for each theory in the existing anxiety, autism, and neuroscience literature". The paper is purely theoretical or a review, with no new data. It is also not about misophonia: it covers only SOR, so not_misophonia/E2 would also apply.

codes.sample: No human participants. The units of analysis are YouTube ASMR channels: the 10 largest mostly English-speaking channels (taken from Bode, 2019) and the 10 largest Mexican channels, with data collected from YouTube on April 6, 2022.
codes.instruments: None. Misophonia was not assessed. The variables are channel metrics only: subscriber count, number of videos, total views, sponsored content, views of the most-viewed sponsored video, likes/comments, and notable sponsors.
codes.note: This is a marketing and media-studies paper about sponsored ASMR videos on YouTube. Misophonia appears only in reference-list titles (Janik & Banissy 2018; Rouw & Erfanian 2018). There are no participants and no misophonia measure. Its design (an analysis of channel metrics) would also fail I1–I3.

codes.sample: 544 social media comments (YouTube 302, Instagram 122, Ekşi Sözlük 120) about a Head & Shoulders ASMR (whispering) TV/online ad in Turkey, collected Oct 2021–Jan 2022. These are comments, not participants, and no demographics are given.
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The study used qualitative and quantitative content analysis of attitude expressions (Aristotle's ethos/pathos/logos framework). No misophonia instrument, interview or criteria.
codes.note: Marketing study of an ASMR ad. Misophonia appears only in the background and in a speculative conclusion: "fısıltılı konuşmanın, reklam izleyicisinde mizofoniyi tetikleyici etki gösterip..." (p.34). No one was assessed or classified for misophonia. The unit of analysis is the comment, not the person. E2 could also apply.

codes.sample: None of its own. This is a Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 RCTs of CBT for adults with tinnitus (2733 participants in total).
codes.instruments: No misophonia instrument. The pooled trials measured tinnitus outcomes (THI, TFI, TQ, TRQ, THQ, TEQ), depression and anxiety (HADS, BDI, PHQ-9, GAD-7), and quality of life (QoLI, SWLS, HUI).
codes.note: Systematic review of RCTs (E4_design, the first exclusion reason that applies). It is also not about misophonia: the text retrieved (first 400,000 of 591,336 characters) never mentions misophonia. Only noise sensitivity, hyperacusis and sound sensitivity appear, as treatment modules or hyperacusis questionnaires. No prevalence data.

codes.sample: None of its own. This is a systematic review of 31 studies (14 tinnitus prevalence studies and 17 genetic association studies; 383,063 patients).
codes.instruments: None for misophonia. The included studies used tinnitus measures such as THI, TFI and self-report items.
codes.note: Systematic review about the genetics of tinnitus. Misophonia comes up only once, in passing: "tinnitus related to misophonia in population-based cohorts [9, 11, 41, 46, 47, 58]" (Discussion, Genetic Signature of Tinnitus). The review reports no misophonia counts. Reference 58 could be checked as a possible primary study.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative review and theoretical paper proposing a cognitive-behavioural model of tinnitus distress.
codes.instruments: None. The paper never mentions misophonia or any misophonia instrument; it discusses only tinnitus measures (TCQ, TQ, THQ, TRQ, TCS, THI, TVAQ, TFAS) and HADS.
codes.note: The abstract says the evidence is "critically reviewed" to propose a model. The paper is also about tinnitus, not misophonia, so not_misophonia would apply too, but E4_design comes first in the order. The full text was checked and contains no misophonia data.

codes.sample: ALSPAC UK population birth cohort; analysis sample of 6,621 children (50.8% female, 95.3% white) who attended the age-11 hearing clinic and had data on at least one outcome. Not recruited for sound sensitivity.
codes.instruments: A single interview question on hyperacusis at age 11: 'ever experience oversensitivity or distress to particular sounds?'. Hyperacusis at age 28 came from the Sussex Screener for Misophonia (SSfM), but it was used only as a correlate (OR), with no misophonia counts. SDQ-E for anxiety.
codes.possible_duplicate: ALSPAC age-11 hyperacusis item, also analysed in Hall, Humphriss, Baguley, Parker & Steer (2016). ALSPAC age-28 SSfM data are in Rinaldi & Simner (2025), which may itself be an eligible misophonia prevalence report.
codes.note: The age-11 item is defined and analysed only as hyperacusis ('distress to particular everyday sounds rather than to loud sounds'). Misophonia comes up only in the Discussion. Hyperacusis: 242/6,621 (3.7%) (Table 1). The reviewer could reconsider if the 'particular sounds' item is judged misophonia-like. For the misophonia data, check the SSfM report.

codes.sample: 164 adults who completed an online survey (Nov–Dec 2021). They were recruited from University of West Georgia psychology students, faculty and staff, social media, and the Rhine Research Center mailing list.
codes.instruments: ASMR-15; Survey of Anomalous Experiences (SAE); a single yes/no synesthesia item (Hartmann, 1991); a single yes/no psychometry item. No misophonia instrument was used.
codes.note: The study is about psychometry, ASMR and synesthesia. Misophonia appears only in Introduction background citations (e.g., "those who report ASMR are more likely to report misophonia (Janik McErlean and Banissy, 2018)"). It was not measured and no counts are reported. E2 does not fit because no sound-tolerance construct was measured either.
